At the beginning of that summer, Erik Refstrup returned from two years in Italy. A sculptor when he left, he came back a painter, already noticed by the public, with paintings sold and commissions for more.

Success had answered almost as soon as he called because he possessed a reliable instinct for his own limits, keeping his art close to his character. His was no expansive, lavish talent, alive with every possibility and seemingly ready to win every crown, a triumphant bacchanalian procession sweeping through all territories, sowing gold everywhere and setting a genius astride every panther! He belonged to those people who have a buried dream within them, a quiet shrine in some corner of the soul where they are at once most themselves and least themselves. A single yearning refrain runs through everything they make. Every work their hands produce carries the same timidly bounded family likeness, as though all were views of one small native country, one sheltered spot far in the mountains. So it was with Erik. Wherever he dived into beauty's ocean, the pearl he brought back into daylight was always the same.

He painted on small canvases: a solitary figure close to the viewer, its own shadow colouring it clay-blue; beyond it a stretch of heath or campagna, and on the horizon a sunset afterglow of reddish yellow. In one painting a young girl is reading her fortune in the Italian manner. She kneels where brown soil shows between clumps of short grass. Having unfastened the hammered-silver heart, cross, and anchor from her necklace, she has scattered them before her. On her knees, she faithfully closes her eyes and shields them with one hand, while reaching with the other towards love's inexpressible ecstasy, sorrow comforted by the cross, or hopeful trust in an ordinary destiny. Her hand has not yet ventured to the earth. It draws back in that cold, mysterious shade. Her face is flushed; her mouth hovers between a prayer and tears. Solemnity fills the scene. Far off, the sunset burns fiercely, almost threateningly; as its light creeps over the heather it becomes softly mournful. “If you only knew—rapture of love beyond words, bitter sorrow solaced by the cross, or the trusting hope of a common fate?”

In another she stands on the brown heath, rigid with desire, her cheek resting against her clasped hands. Her innocent yearning is sweet, tinged with sadness and a little resentment that life should overlook her. Why hasn't Eros arrived with his roses of kisses? Does he believe she is still too young? Oh, if only he would feel how her heart is pounding! If he would place his hand against it! Inside lies a world, a whole world of worlds, waiting to wake. Why doesn't it call aloud? It remains a bud, folded tightly about its sweetness and its beauty, existing for itself alone and weighed down by itself. It senses something in life beyond its knowledge. That unknown thing has warmed the enclosing petals and illuminated the deepest heart of crimson dusk. There the perfume is not yet perfume, only a presentiment compressed into a single trembling tear!

Will it never escape, breathe out its sleeping fragrance, and possess the riches that already belong to it? Will it never open, never blush into waking as bright sunbeams pierce beneath its petals? Her patience with Eros is exhausted! Tears are gathering behind the quiver of her lips. She stares into emptiness in a hopeless challenge, while her small head droops ever more dejectedly. Its fine profile turns inward towards the painted scene, where a mild breeze carries red dust across dark broom beneath a sky the golden colour of sherry.

This was Erik's painting. Whenever he expressed what he had to say, pictures of this sort emerged. At times other visions came to him, and he wanted to escape the narrow ring in which he worked. Yet each experiment beyond his limits, each trial of his gifts elsewhere, ended in his retreat, cold with discouragement, convinced he had borrowed somebody else's property and made something that wasn't his. These unsuccessful ventures taught him more than he realized, but afterward he became Erik Refstrup more intensely than ever. With renewed daring and an almost painful ardour he surrendered to the worship of his own individuality. Religious enthusiasm coloured the whole way he lived with himself, down to his smallest gesture. He seemed attended by misty crowds of lovely figures: younger sisters to Parmigianino's slim-limbed women, with long throats and broad, slender princess hands. They sat with him at his table and filled his glass with nobly graceful movements, holding him captive in their beautiful dreams through Luini's mysterious, meditative smile, so subtly unreadable in its puzzling sweetness.

Yet after eleven days of loyal service to this god, other forces would sometimes take command. A fierce appetite for crude, bodily pleasures seized him. He plunged into debauchery, fevered by that human urge to destroy oneself which, when the blood burns at its hottest, hungers for abasement, perversity, dirt, and obscenity. Its strength exactly matches another longing just as human: the longing to remain larger than oneself, and cleaner.

In such moods almost nothing was sufficiently coarse or violent for him. Once they passed, recovering his equilibrium took a long time. These excesses were, in truth, foreign to his nature. He was too sound for them, too little infected by brooding. They were something like a recoil from his dedication to art's higher spirits, almost an act of vengeance: as if those lofty purposes that choice, assisted by circumstances, had given him were an injury done to his nature.

This double conflict did not proceed in clear enough outlines to show upon the outward course of Erik Refstrup's days, nor did he want his friends to understand this side of him. Outwardly he remained the same uncomplicated, easygoing fellow as before: a little clumsy in his aversion to spoken emotion, something of a freebooter when it came to grasping and keeping. The other life was there nonetheless. In quiet moments one sometimes sensed it, like bells tolling from a drowned city beneath the sea. Never had he and Niels understood one another better. Each knew it and silently pledged himself anew to their old friendship. When the holiday season came and Niels felt he must finally pay his long-postponed visit to Aunt Rosalie, Consul Claudi's wife in Fjordby, Erik accompanied him.

The high road from the prosperous country above Fjordby reaches the town between two enormous hawthorn hedges. One encloses Consul Claudi's kitchen garden, the other his extensive ornamental garden beside the shore. Where the road goes afterward is open to debate. Does it finish in the Consul's yard, big enough to be a marketplace? Or continue round a bend between his timber yard and hayloft, eventually becoming the town's principal street? Many travellers follow the curve and keep driving. Many others consider their journey finished once they pass through his broad, tarred gateway, where the doors stand perpetually open and skins spread out to dry cover them.

All the buildings were old except the high warehouse, whose lifeless-looking slate roof was Fjordby's latest architectural novelty. Three large gables seemed to press the long, low main house down onto its knees. A shadowed corner connected it to the kitchen and stable wing; another, brighter corner linked it to the warehouse. In the dark angle lay the shop's back entrance. The shop, peasants' waiting-room, office, and servants' hall made up a dim little world to themselves. Cheap tobacco, damp wool, spices, dried cod, and musty floorboards mingled there in an atmosphere so dense that one could almost taste it. Cross the office, with its sharp sealing-wax fumes, however, and reach the passage separating family life from business, and an overriding scent of new millinery prepared the visitor for the subtler perfume of the living-rooms. No bouquet, no actual blossom, supplied it. It was that elusive, memory-filled air peculiar to a home, whose source nobody can identify. Each home has its own. It may recall any of a thousand things, old gloves, fresh playing cards, a piano left open; yet it is never quite the same. Cigars, incense, and scent may smother it, but cannot destroy it. It returns unaltered, present as it always was. Here its character was floral, though neither roses nor stock nor any flower with a name: more like the imagined fragrance of the strange pale-sapphire lilies that wind their blossoms around antique porcelain vases. How perfectly it belonged to these broad, low-ceilinged rooms, their inherited furnishings and formal, old-world elegance! The floors possessed the whiteness found only on grandmothers' floors. The walls wore a single colour, with a slender pattern of pale garlands beneath the ceiling and its central plaster rose. Fluted doors had polished brass handles shaped like dolphins. Small square windowpanes were screened by snow-white gauze curtains, their gathered fullness tied with flirtatious bows of coloured ribbon, fit to enclose Corydon and Phyllis's marriage bed. Old-fashioned flowers grew on the sills in green pots of differing shades: blue agapanthus and Canterbury bells, delicate-leaved myrtles, scarlet verbenas, and geraniums as vivid as butterflies. Above all, though, the furnishings defined the rooms. There were tables too heavy to shift, offering wide surfaces of darkened mahogany; chairs whose backs curved about the sitter; and cupboards in every imaginable shape. Great dressers carried pale yellow wooden inlays of mythological subjects, Daphne, Arachne, Narcissus. Small writing desks stood on slender, twisted legs, with a dendrite-marble mosaic on each tiny drawer showing a pretty square house beside a tree. All dated from before Napoleon. Mirrors bore white or bronze paintings on their glass: reeds and lotus floating on a luminous sea. The sofa was certainly no flimsy four-legged thing meant for two. It rose solidly from the floor, massive as a spacious terrace. A console-cupboard, built into the sofa itself, stood on each side. Above each rose a smaller cabinet, architectural in effect, reaching a man's height and supporting a treasured old jar well beyond careless fingers. Such an abundance of antiques in the Consul's house was natural enough: his father and grandfather had both rested and enjoyed life's comforts here between their labours in the timber yard and office.

His grandfather, Berendt Berendtsen Claudi, whose name the business still carried, had erected the buildings and chiefly concerned himself with shopkeeping and produce. His father expanded the timber trade, purchased farmland, built the hayloft, and established both gardens. The present Claudi enlarged the grain business and put up the warehouse. Besides his commercial concerns, he served as English and Hanoverian vice-consul and as agent for Lloyd's. Between grain and the Western Sea he was too busy to give the other departments more than a passing glance. He shared their oversight between a bankrupt cousin and an elderly, impossible steward. Every so often the steward cornered him by insisting that the farm must be worked, whatever became of the shop. When ploughing was needed they could find horses for timber-hauling wherever they liked; they weren't getting his, that he swore. But the fellow knew his business, so tolerating him was the only course.

In his early fifties, Consul Claudi cut a substantial figure. His regular features, so strong they bordered on coarse, could set readily into cool shrewdness and determination, or soften just as readily into a nearly greedy expression, as though tasting some delicious morsel. Indeed, he was equally comfortable bargaining with sharp-witted peasants, disputing with an obstinate salvage crew, or lingering over the final bottle of port among grey-bearded sinners. There he listened to decidedly indecent tales or told them himself with the colourful directness for which he was famous.
That, though, was only part of his character.

His upbringing understandably made him feel outside his territory whenever discussion strayed beyond strictly practical subjects. Yet he neither ridiculed things he failed to grasp nor concealed what he didn't know. Still less would he have thought of pronouncing an opinion and demanding deference merely because he was an experienced, mature citizen who paid substantial taxes. Quite the opposite: when women and younger men discussed such subjects, he often listened with an almost touching respect. Occasionally he ventured a tentative question, preceded by elaborate apologies. This nearly always brought an answer of scrupulous care, for which he thanked the speaker with that gracious courtesy an older man's gratitude towards the young can have.

At particularly favourable moments Consul Claudi could show an unexpectedly delicate quality: a yearning in his clear brown gaze, a sad smile about his firm mouth, a searching, recollective sound in his voice. It was as if he longed for a different, and to his mind finer, world than the one his friends and acquaintances assigned him to, body and soul.

His wife acted as envoy between him and that finer world. She belonged to those pale, mild, virginal characters who lack the courage, or perhaps the desire, to pour out love so completely that not a scrap of self remains in the soul's most private chamber. Not even for an instant can feeling carry them into the blind ecstasy of flinging themselves beneath their idol's chariot. That they cannot do. Everything else, though, they can do for the one they love. They undertake the harshest duties, stand ready for the costliest sacrifices, and shrink from no degradation. At least, the finest among them are like this.

Mrs. Claudi had not been required to endure trials of that kind. Her marriage nevertheless contained sorrows. Everyone in Fjordby knew the Consul was hardly the most faithful of husbands, or had not been until a few years earlier, and had fathered several children outside marriage in the neighbourhood. Naturally this caused her bitter suffering. Holding her heart steady through the uproar of jealousy, disgust, rage, shame, and nauseating fear had been difficult; she had felt the ground sliding beneath her. Yet she held firm. Not only did she never speak a reproach, she also prevented her husband from confessing, from asking outright for pardon, from saying anything resembling a penitent promise. She felt that once words were allowed, their force might carry her away from him. She would endure quietly. Within that quiet she tried to persuade herself she shared responsibility for his wrongdoing, because she had surrounded herself with a barrier that her love had lacked the power to destroy. She enlarged this fault in her own eyes until she felt a vague need to be pardoned herself. Eventually her conduct brought rumours that the girls Consul Claudi had seduced, and their children, were being helped with more than cash. An unseen woman's hand seemed to be protecting them, guarding them against trouble, and providing support and direction.
Thus goodness came out of wrongdoing, and the saint and the sinner each helped the other become better.

The Claudis' two children were a boy employed in a Hamburg merchant's office and a daughter of nineteen. Fennimore, the daughter, took her name from the heroine of _St. Roche_, a novel by Frau von Palzow much admired when Mrs. Claudi was a girl.

On the day the steamer brought Niels and Erik into Fjordby, the Consul and Fennimore waited to meet them. Discovering his cousin was pretty delighted Niels. Previously he had seen her only in an appalling old family daguerreotype, where she loomed through mist beside her brother and parents, all with feverishly crimson cheeks and jewellery picked out in shiny gold. Now he thought her utterly lovely, standing in her light morning gown and delicate shoes, their black ribbons crossing the white stockings over her insteps. One foot rested on the plank bordering the quay. Leaning forward with a smile, she offered him the handle of her parasol in greeting, a substitute handshake before the vessel was secured. How red her mouth was, how white her teeth, how finely her brow and temples were shaped beneath the broad Eugenie hat. Deep black lace, weighted with glittering jet, shaded its edges.

When the gangway finally descended, the Consul set off with Erik. He had already introduced himself across twelve feet of water and, still shouting, involved Erik in a comic discussion of seasickness and its torments with a shrivelled hatter's widow aboard the boat. Now he directed Erik's admiration towards the great lime trees in front of the revenue collector's home, and the new schooner awaiting launch at Thomas Rasmussen's yard.

Fennimore walked beside Niels. She showed him the garden flag raised to welcome him and his companion, then they began talking about the Neergaards in Copenhagen. They soon agreed that Mrs. Neergaard was rather—just a little—neither supplied the adjective. Instead Fennimore gave a prim smile and curled her hand in a feline gesture. Both evidently understood: they smiled, then promptly grew grave again. They continued in silence, each wondering what impression the other was receiving.

Fennimore had expected Niels Lyhne to be taller, more distinguished-looking, with a more emphatic individuality, like a word underlined. He, meanwhile, had discovered far more than he had anticipated. She seemed delightful to him, almost seductive, despite a dress a little too suggestive of provincial smartness. Once indoors, she stood in the hall with lowered eyes and an absent-minded air, removing her hat and arranging her hair. Her hands and wrists turned with such wonderfully soft, languid grace that gratitude rose in him as though she had caressed him. This nearly bewildering feeling of thankfulness stayed with him all that day and the next. Sometimes it rose so warmly and strongly that he thought nothing could make him happier than thanking her aloud for her beauty and sweetness.

Both Erik and Niels quickly felt at ease in the Consul's welcoming home. Within a few days they had settled into the pleasantly ordered laziness that makes a proper holiday, and that well-intentioned friends so easily invade. It took all their tact to escape the oppressive evening gatherings, grand boating parties, summer dances, and amateur plays continually threatening their tranquillity. They almost wished house and garden stood on an uninhabited island. Robinson Crusoe could scarcely have been more alarmed by the footprints in the sand than they were by unfamiliar overcoats in the hall or strangers' little handbags on the sitting-room table. They preferred keeping to themselves. Before the first week's midpoint, both had fallen in love with Fennimore. This was not yet the grown passion that insists on knowing its prospects, that yearns for possession and certainty. It was only love's earliest light, like spring sensed in the air, full of a longing close to sadness and an unrest that beats gently with pleasure. The heart becomes pliable, tender, easily stirred. Light glancing on water, leaves whispering, a blossom opening: all acquire an unfamiliar power. Unnamed and indistinct hopes burst forth, suddenly bathing the world in sunshine, then disappear as quickly. Feeble discouragement drifts like a broad cloud over that radiance, churning hope's bright flashes into its grey wake. Then comes despair, melting despair: a sweetly bitter submission to destiny, a heart absorbed in pity for itself, renunciation admiring its image in soft elegies and swooning into a partly theatrical sigh.... Yet the roses whisper again. A dreamed-of country emerges from fog, golden mist hanging over tender beech tops, fragrant summer shade beneath branches that arch above pathways leading nobody knows where.

One evening, after tea, everyone sat together in the sitting-room. Pouring rain ruled out the garden and every outdoor diversion, but nobody appeared troubled. Being confined indoors lent the room the cosy ease of a winter night. Besides, the rain was a blessing. Everything had been dried and scorched, and now water rushed down. The big drops drumming on the frame of the window reflector suggested brief, indistinct visions of juicy green pastures and revived leaves. Now and then someone murmured, “How it pours!” and looked towards the glass with a small gleam of satisfaction, half-consciously luxuriating in sympathy with all the growing things outside. Erik brought out the mandolin he had carried home from Italy and sang of Napoli and glittering stars. Then a young woman who had joined them for tea sat at the piano and accompanied herself in “My little nook among the mountains.” She sang in Swedish, opening her _ah's_ extravagantly to produce the proper Swedish flavour.
Not especially sensitive to music, Niels let it lull him into a mild sadness and drifted into his own reflections. Then Fennimore started singing.
He came out of his reverie, but without pleasure.

Her singing unsettled him painfully. Under the enchantment of her own voice, she ceased to be the little provincial girl. How strangely the notes swept her away, how openly and without restraint she gave herself to them! He felt almost that it was indecent, that she was stripping herself bare in song before his eyes. Heat gathered round his heart and pulsed in his temples; he lowered his gaze. Could nobody else perceive it? No, they noticed nothing. Yet she had escaped herself, escaped Fjordby and its poetry and its feelings! She had entered a wider, more daring country, where passions flourished on mountain summits and scattered crimson flowers into the tempest.

Was his poor understanding of music making him hear too much in her voice? He could scarcely believe that explanation, though he wanted to, since he greatly preferred her ordinary self. Sitting over her needlework, speaking in her level, peaceful tone, or raising her gentle, clear eyes, she drew his whole nature towards her with the compelling force of a profound, tranquil homesickness. He wanted to abase himself before her, kneel, and call her sacred. He continually longed to approach her more closely, not only the person she was now, but the child she had been, every day of her life before he knew her. Whenever they were alone he encouraged her to speak of earlier times, the little sorrows and errors and foolish fancies belonging to every childhood. He dwelled within these recollections, grasping them with uneasy jealousy and a tender hunger to possess, to merge with, these pale first sketches of a life already glowing with fuller, riper colour. Then came the startling force of that song! It shocked him like a broad horizon suddenly opening at a bend in a path. The wooded hollow he had considered home shrank to one small part of the view; its modest undulations became trivial beside the magnificence of the hills and far-off moorlands. But surely the view was a _fata morgana_, what he thought he heard in her voice a mere illusion. Already she was speaking as she always spoke, restored to her blessed familiar self. A thousand small signs assured him, too, that she resembled quiet water, untroubled by storms or waves, mirroring the blue sky and its stars.

That was the woman he loved and the woman he saw. In his company she slowly adapted herself to his vision, without deliberately pretending: his idea of her was partly accurate, after all. Every glance and word, every wish and thought of his, addressed and revered that side of her. Naturally she adopted the appearance he all but imposed. Besides, how could she trouble herself to give everyone an exact portrait of her character when her mind circled only one person: Erik, her one and only, her chosen master? She loved him with a passion that seemed to come from outside herself, an idolatry that frightened her. She had expected love to be a gentle dignity, instead of this devouring agitation of fear, abasement, and uncertainty. Many times, when a declaration appeared ready on Erik's lips, she had felt she ought to cover his mouth and forbid it. She ought to accuse herself, explain her deception, explain how little she deserved his love: how small and earthly and unclean she was, how far from anything noble, how miserably base and ordinary and wicked! Beneath his admiring eyes she felt fraudulent. When she failed to keep away, she felt scheming. At night she felt guilty because she could not bring herself to pray that God would turn Erik's heart elsewhere, leaving his life all brightness, honour, and glory. She knew her ignoble passion would pull him down.

Erik loved her almost against his will. The woman of his ideal had always been lofty, proud, and noble, her pale face touched with a still sadness, the chill of a temple lingering in the austere folds of her clothes. Fennimore's sweetness defeated that image. Her beauty was impossible to resist. A fresh, unknowing sensuality breathed from her whole person. Her walk whispered of the body beneath; her movements suggested nakedness, while her stillness spoke with a dreamy eloquence. She could help neither, could neither disguise one nor hush the other, even if she had been at all aware of them. Erik perceived this more clearly than anyone and knew very well how much of her appeal lay in physical loveliness alone. He resisted it, for his soul contained elevated conceptions of love, perhaps drawn not just from poetry and tradition but from levels of his own nature deeper than those visible on the surface. Wherever they came from, though, those ideals had to give way.

Before he had told Fennimore of his love, the good ship _Berendt Claudi_ arrived. She was bound farther up the fjord to discharge her cargo, so she anchored in the channel instead of entering harbour. The Consul was proud of his schooner and eager to display her to his visitors. One afternoon they therefore rowed out to take tea aboard.

The weather was splendid, utterly windless, and everyone was determined to enjoy themselves. Time slipped away. They drank English porter, bit into rounds of English hardtack as big as moons, and ate salted mackerel taken during the North Sea crossing. They worked the ship's pump until water foamed, tilted the compass, used the big tin siphon to draw water out of barrels, and heard the mate play his eight-sided hand harmonica.
Night had properly fallen before they thought of going ashore.

They divided into two groups. Erik, Fennimore, and two older members of the company took the ship's yawl. It would circle the harbour before making a leisurely return to shore. Everyone else took the Consul's boat, bound straight for the pier. The idea was to discover how singing sounded across the water on so still a night. Erik and Fennimore consequently sat side by side in the yawl's stern, with the mandolin between them. But when the oars entered the water, an extraordinarily brilliant phosphorescence appeared. It captivated them, and they forgot the music.

The boat moved on without a sound. Behind it the dark, glasslike surface opened into changing furrows and rings of delicate white light. That glow was too weak to illuminate the darkness outside its own track, except when it seemed briefly to release a luminous vapour. White foam sprang up at each oar stroke, falling astern in quivering circles that faded by degrees. Shining droplets scattered off the blades like a phosphorescent shower, going dark in the air but rekindling the water wherever they landed. The fjord was so quiet that the oars seemed merely to divide the stillness into equal intervals. Soft grey dusk brooded over the noiseless depths. Boat and passengers blended into a single dark shape, from which the glowing water picked out the moving oars, occasionally a rope trailing overboard, or perhaps the rower's impassive brown face. Nobody said anything. Fennimore trailed her hand in the cool water. She and Erik turned to watch the shining net sliding silently behind them, their thoughts caught in its lovely meshes.
Someone on shore shouted for music and broke their reverie. Together they sang two or three Italian romances, accompanying themselves on the mandolin.
Afterward the quiet settled over everything again.

Finally they reached the small landing that projected from the garden. The Consul's boat lay empty beside it; the others had already gone indoors. Fennimore's aunt and the remaining passenger followed them, but Erik and Fennimore stayed, watching the yawl head back to the ship. The garden gate clicked shut. Gradually the oar strokes became inaudible and the wash around the landing subsided. Then a breath passed through the black trees nearby, like a concealed sigh that lifted the leaves gently before flying away and leaving them by themselves.

Together they turned from the fjord and faced one another. He took her hand, drew her slowly towards him as if asking a question, and kissed her. “Fennimore!” he breathed. They began walking through the darkened garden.
“You've known for so long!” he said. “Yes,” she answered. They continued, and once again the gate clicked closed.
After coffee with the others and good-nights at the front door, Erik finally reached his bedroom, but sleep would not come.
The room felt airless. He pushed the windows open as far as they would go, stretched out on the couch, and listened.
He longed to be outside once more.

How loudly every sound travelled through the house! He heard the Consul padding in slippers. Now Mrs. Claudi was opening the kitchen door to check that the fire had been extinguished. Whatever did Niels need from his trunk at this hour! Ah, a mouse was moving behind the panelling. Someone crossed the attic without shoes, then someone else: two people. Finally! He opened the door into the adjoining guest-room and paused to listen. Then he quietly raised its window, swung his legs across the sill, and lowered himself into the yard. The mangling-room, he knew, gave access to the shore. If he met anyone, he would explain that he had left his mandolin beside the landing and was retrieving it before the dew spoiled it. Accordingly he put the mandolin across his back.
The garden had brightened slightly. A little wind stirred, and a small piece of moon stretched a trembling silver ribbon between the landing and the _Berendt Claudi_.

He crossed the garden and climbed onto the sloping stonework guarding it from the water. It turned in sharp corners round a broad embankment and continued all the way to the harbour breakwater's end. Awkwardly balancing on the flat, tilted stones, he finally gained the end of the mole and sat on its bench, somewhat breathless.
Overhead the harbour lamp's red lantern swung gently to and fro, making an iron sighing sound. The flag rope tapped lightly against the pole.

A little more moon appeared, laying a tentative grey-white glow over the motionless ships and the town's jumble of square roofs and pale gables with dark window eyes. Beyond them all the church tower rose, light and serene.

He reclined in a dream as an indescribable surge of joy and triumph filled his heart. He felt wealthy, strong, warm with life. Surely Fennimore must hear every loving thought that grew out of his ecstasy, vines twining together, blossom following blossom. He stood, struck the mandolin strings briskly, and sang in triumph towards the sleeping town:
“_Wakeful aloft lies my lassie, She listens to my song!_”
Whenever his heart overflowed, he returned to the old ballad's words, singing them over and over.

Little by little his excitement quietened. Recollections crowded in of earlier hours when he had felt most helpless, poorest, most abandoned. They brought a small taut ache, like the sensation of tears first gathering behind the eyes. He sat back on the bench. His hand rested silently across the mandolin strings while he looked over the fjord's blue-grey breadth. Moonlight made a sparkling bridge beyond the dark ship towards the outlines of the Morsö hills, a faint, mournful country of cloud-blue drawn through a whitish haze.
The memories kept coming, but softened, rising into lovelier countries where the glow of a rosy sunrise seemed to fall on them.
... _My lassie!_
Quietly, for himself, he sang:
“_Wakeful aloft lies my lassie, She listens to my song._”
